issues.explanation: 'People cycling' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile for a refugee trauma presentation when the other triggers are funerals/graves and car sounds, and there are no corresponding memory or appraisal items suggesting bicycles or a cycling-related trauma cue. This trigger looks clinically disconnected from the stated trauma context and the rest of the network.

'I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. In an older married male refugee with severe PTSD symptoms, self-harm can occur, but here it is the only extreme behavioral regulation item and is unsupported by the other selected strategies, memories, or appraisals. It appears clinically out of pattern relative to the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation.

vignette:
Rajan Chaudhary is a 75-year-old South Asian man who came to the United States as a refugee decades ago and has spent the better part of his adult life working as a potter in a small studio attached to his home in a mid-sized American city. He lives with his wife of fifty years. He was referred for psychological assessment after his primary care physician noted significant functional decline and persistent sleep disturbance, and after Rajan himself, at his wife's quiet insistence, finally admitted that something had been wrong for a very long time.

The events that brought Rajan to this country unfolded across several months of communal violence in the region where he was born. He was in his mid-twenties when the killing began. What he carries most viscerally from that period is not a single moment but a sustained atmosphere of terror - the sound of vehicles moving slowly through narrow streets at night, which always preceded raids; the sight of uniformed men moving through his neighbourhood with absolute authority, deciding who stayed and who did not; and, above all, the funerals. There were many funerals in those months, held quickly and without ceremony, bodies lowered into earth while families looked over their shoulders. Rajan helped carry at least three of those bodies. He does not speak of this directly. He has never been able to find the words for what those weeks were, and when he tries, the images come not as a narrative but as shards - a specific quality of light, the sound of a car engine idling, the colour of a uniform - arriving without context or sequence, feeling, he has said, more present and more real than anything that happened yesterday.

He arrived in the United States and built a life. The potter's wheel became the organizing principle of that life: the discipline of clay, the patience it required, the way a form could be coaxed into being over hours. For many years, work was also a kind of refuge. But over the past several years, and with increasing intensity in the last eighteen months, Rajan has found himself unable to sustain the concentration that throwing requires. He sits at the wheel and his hands, which once moved with practiced certainty, falter. He has come to believe that he is no longer the craftsman he was - that whatever defined him as a maker of things has been taken from him - and this belief sits in him like a stone. Several commissions have gone unfulfilled. A gallery relationship he had maintained for over two decades has quietly ended.

Outside the studio, his world has contracted around a set of arrangements that feel, to him, like simple common sense. He does not attend funerals. When a neighbour died last spring and his wife asked him to accompany her to the service, he told her he was unwell, and she did not press him. He avoids the cemetery that sits four blocks from their home, rerouting his walks without ever explaining why. When he hears a car idling outside - especially at night, especially a heavier engine - he moves to a window and stands there, scanning the street methodically, watching until the vehicle leaves. He does the same in public spaces: his eyes move continuously across exits, across faces, across anything that might signal what is coming. When a police officer is visible - at a crossroads, outside a store - Rajan will cross the street or wait, and he has told his wife only that he finds such encounters uncomfortable. He has declined several family celebrations in recent years, including a grandchild's birthday gathering, because he was certain that feeling happy or hopeful in such settings would be followed by something terrible. The logic feels unassailable to him. He has also stopped voicing any disagreement, even mild, in family conversations, having concluded that he cannot manage the aftermath of conflict - that even the smallest upset now exceeds what he is capable of bearing.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a moment at the wheel three weeks ago when he simply stopped, sat with his hands in wet clay, and wept without knowing why. He has told his therapist that he does not expect to feel better - he is not sure he believes that is possible - but that he would like, before he dies, to finish one more piece of work that he is proud of.
